name: AWS Application Load Balancer
summary: AWS’s managed layer-7 load balancer: routes HTTP requests by host, path or header to EC2, containers, IPs or Lambda.
intro: An Application Load Balancer (ALB) is one of the Elastic Load Balancing types. It lives in your VPC, with a node in each Availability Zone you enable. A listener accepts connections on a port, say HTTPS on 443, and terminates TLS. Its rules are checked in priority order: each matches on host name, path, HTTP header, method, query string or source IP, then forwards to a target group, redirects, or returns a fixed response. A target group holds the actual backends (instances by ID, IP addresses, or a single Lambda function) and runs its own health checks.

Because it understands HTTP, one ALB can front many services: `/api/*` to one container service, `admin.example.com` to another. It supports HTTP/2, gRPC and WebSockets, can sign users in through any OpenID Connect provider before a request reaches your app, and scales its own capacity with traffic. You pay about $0.0225 an hour (roughly $16 a month in US East) plus Load Balancer Capacity Units, measured by whichever is highest of new connections, active connections, bytes processed and rule evaluations.
strengths: Content-based routing lets one load balancer and one certificate serve many services
Integrates with Auto Scaling groups and ECS, which register and deregister targets for you
Built-in OIDC or Cognito sign-in, AWS WAF attachment and access logs
Can invoke Lambda functions directly, so small HTTP endpoints don’t need API Gateway
limits: Regional only: multi-region failover needs Route 53 or Global Accelerator on top
Clients reach it by DNS name, not by addresses you choose; for static IPs to allow-list, put Global Accelerator or a Network Load Balancer in front
Default quotas of 100 rules and 1,000 targets per load balancer, and at most 5 condition values per rule
The hourly charge runs whether or not there’s traffic, which adds up across many small environments

story: AWS launched Elastic Load Balancing in May 2009, together with CloudWatch and Auto Scaling, so EC2 customers could spread traffic over instances the way Amazon already did internally. That original balancer could speak HTTP, but it sent every request to the same pool of instances on a fixed port. As teams split apps into microservices and packed several containers onto each instance with Amazon ECS, one pool per load balancer meant one load balancer per service.

On 11 August 2016 AWS added a second type, the Application Load Balancer, and renamed the original the Classic Load Balancer. The ALB reads each HTTP request and picks a target group by its URL path, so `/api` and `/mobile` could go to different services that “can run and be scaled independently”, as Jeff Barr put it in the launch post. It also brought WebSockets and HTTP/2, and an hourly price 10% below Classic.

Over the next years the ALB grew into a small HTTP router: host-based routing in 2017, sign-in through OpenID Connect and redirects in 2018, Lambda functions as targets the same year, and gRPC in 2020. Classic Load Balancers still run, but the ALB became AWS’s main HTTP load balancer.

choices.choice: Route by request content, not just by port
choices.why: Microservices need different paths to reach different fleets. Matching rules on the path (and later host, header, method, query and source IP) lets one load balancer and one certificate front many services.

choices.choice: Target groups of ports, not lists of instances
choices.why: ECS runs several containers per instance, each on its own port. Registering instance-and-port pairs, each with its own health check, let the scheduler add and remove containers without a load balancer per service.

choices.choice: Bill by capacity units, not just hours and bytes
choices.why: Workloads stress a load balancer differently: a WebSocket app holds many idle connections, a download site moves bytes. An LCU charges for whichever dimension you use most.
Added in 2018 so an HTTP app could run serverless behind the same load balancer, and the same path rules, as its container services.

timeline.text: Elastic Load Balancing launches with CloudWatch and Auto Scaling
Application Load Balancer launches on 11 August; the original becomes “Classic”
Host-based routing and IP targets; the Network Load Balancer covers layer 4
OIDC and Cognito sign-in, redirects, fixed responses and Lambda targets
JWT validation, URL and host rewrites, and Target Optimizer concurrency limits
